extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical mechanics / fluid dynamics (readers of Newtonian mechanics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted laws and principles from a classical mechanics treatise (Latin) concerning similarity/scaling of motions, resistance of bodies in rare and continuous media, shape effects on resistance, and efflux of fluids from vessels. Useful for applying scaling laws and classical efflux (Torricelli-type) results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity scaling of motions
rubrics_metrics.description: si duo sint ejusmodi systemata, particulse correspondentes, ... simul moveri ... tempora erunt proportionalia
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two systems are similar and corresponding particles are similarly placed, and magnitudes & densities of corresponding parts are in proportion, then their motions will be similar and occur in proportional times. (Used to deduce how geometrically similar systems scale in time and space; underlies many subsequent scaling corollaries.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance composite scaling (velocity, diameter, density)
rubrics_metrics.description: systematum partes majores resistuntur in ratione composita ex duplicata ratione velocitatum suarum & duplicata ratione diametrorum & ratione densitatis partium systematum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resistance of the larger parts of systems is in the composite ratio formed by the duplicate (square) ratio of their velocities, the duplicate ratio of their diameters, and the ratio of the densities of the parts of the systems. (Derived by combining contributions from centripetal-type forces and from collisions/reflections of particles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate quadratic velocity dependence in elastic fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: Proinde in eodem fluido projectile velox resistentiam patitur, quae est in duplicata ratione velocitatis quam proxime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an elastic fluid like air, a rapidly moving projectile experiences resistance approximately proportional to the square of its velocity. The text explains limiting arguments showing this holds 'quam proxime' for high speeds where interacting forces scale with v^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-speed limit: centrifugally-determined resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporis in fluido quovis elastlco velocissime moti eadem fere est resistentia ac si partes fluldi virlbus suis centrifugis destituentur, seque mutuo non fugerent : si modo fluidi vis elastica ex particularum viribus centrifugis oriatur, & velocitas adeo magna sit ut vires non habeant satis temporis ad agendum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When bodies move extremely fast, their resistance approximates the case where fluid particles have no time to move away (i.e., behave as if centrifugal interactions were absent); this provides a high-speed asymptote for resistance calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance ∝ diameter^2 for similar, equal-velocity bodies in non-evacuating media
rubrics_metrics.description: cum reslstentise similium & sequalium & sequivelocium corporum, in medio cujus partes distantes se mutuo non fugiunt, sint ut quadrata diametrorum
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For similar bodies of equal velocity in a medium whose particles do not flee one another, resistances scale approximately as the square of their diameters. (Used for comparing resistances of geometrically similar projectiles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of origin of medium elasticity on resistance magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Haec omnia ita se habent in fluidis, quorum vis elastica ex particularum viribus centrifugis originem ducit. Quod si vis illa aliunde oriatur ... resistentia ... erit major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the medium's elastic restoring forces originate by mechanisms other than centrifugal particle interactions (e.g., expansion forces of particles), the medium is effectively less 'subtle' and resistance will be greater than in the centrifugal-origin case. (Qualitative guidance about how medium microphysics affects macroscopic resistance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere vs cylinder resistance ratio (equal diameters, cylinder axis motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si globus & cylifidrus cequalibus diametris ... secundum plagam axis cylindri, cequali cum velocitate moveantur: erit resistentia globi duplo minor quam resistentia cytindri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sphere moving along the axis of a cylinder of equal diameter experiences half the resistance of that cylinder, under the idealized rare medium assumptions used (particles equal, equally spaced, interactions considered as impulsive). The proposition is proved by geometric comparison of intercepted particle effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shape influence on resistance; parabolic/elliptic revolution shapes reduce resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Eadem methodo figurae allae Inter se quoad resistentiam comparari possunt, eaeque InvenlrI quae ad motus suos In mediis reslstentibus continuandos aptiores sunt. ... solidum ... generetur, minus resistitur quam solidum prius ... Quam quidem propositionem in construendis navibus non inutilem futuram esse censeo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shapes generated by revolving certain curves (e.g., appropriate parabolic/elliptic profiles, tangency conditions given) can be made to offer smaller resistance than circular solids of the same lengths/widths; this has direct application to ship hull design and minimizing form resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of sphere resistance on particle reflection (resilience) — three cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Cas. 1/2/3: considerentur particulae medii vi reflexionis quam maxima resil[i]ant ... non reflectantur ... vi reflexionis mediocri aliqua resiliant ... & resistentia globi erit in eadem ratione mediocri inter resistentiam in primo casu & resistentiam in secundo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing the resistance of a sphere in a medium of discrete particles, the amount of momentum transferred depends on how particles reflect (maximally elastic, non-reflecting, or intermediate). Maximal reflection yields one value (case 1), no reflection yields a smaller value (case 2), and intermediate resilience produces an intermediate resistance (case 3). Use these cases to bracket physical resistance depending on collision physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere resistance proportionalities (velocity^2, diameter^2, medium density)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 2: Resistentia globi, caeteris paribus, est in duplicata ratione velocitatis. Corol. 3: ... in duplicata ratione diametri. Corol. 4: ... est ut densitas medii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit corollaries state that, ceteris paribus, the resistance of a sphere scales as velocity squared, as diameter squared, and is proportional to the medium's density. Combined, these yield the composite scaling R ∝ ρ d^2 v^2 (as earlier stated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of deceleration via hyperbolic area (retardation formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sit tempus quo globus per resistentiam suam uniformiter continuatam totum suum motum amittere potest ... per punctum C asymptotis AD, AB describatur hyperbola CF. ... area hyperbolica B C F E est ad rectangulum BCGE in hac proportione ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The motion (retardation) of a sphere under constant resistance can be represented geometrically: the distance lost and velocity decay relate to areas under a hyperbola vs rectangle, giving logarithmic relations. The text gives a construction linking total motion lost in time T to areas under a hyperbola and provides a logarithmic proportionality (useful for integrating deceleration laws when R ∝ v^2 or when resistance varies with v).

rubrics_metrics.name: In continuous fluids (water, oil, mercury) sphere resistance is smaller due to limited local interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: In mediis autem continuis quali sunt aqua, oleum calidum, & argentum vivum, in quibus globus non incidit immediate in omnes fluidi particulas ... sed premit tantum proximas particulas & hae premunt alias ... resistentia est adhuc duplo minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In continuous fluids, the sphere does not directly impart momentum to all fluid particles but pushes adjacent layers which transmit motion; under these conditions the effective resistance is still around half (compared with the discrete maximal-reflection case), and for very fluid media resistance diminishes only little with particle fineness. The text suggests different effective multiplicative factors in continuous media and gives an estimate (e.g., sphere must traverse 'octo tertias' [8/3] of its diameter to lose motion in certain cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Efflux velocity equals that acquired by falling from head (Torricelli's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: velocitas aquae effluentis per foramen ... ea erit quam aqua cadendo ab / & casu suo describendo altitudinem IG acquirere potest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The velocity of efflux through a hole in the bottom (or side) of a vessel equals the velocity a body would gain by falling from the free-surface height above the hole. The text provides geometric setup and multiple cases showing this holds regardless of hole position (bottom, side, offset).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of efflux velocity from hole shape and position
rubrics_metrics.description: Eadem est aquse velocitas effluentis per foramen in latere vasis. ... Eadem est aquae effluentis velocitas sive figura foraminis sit circularis sive quadrata vel triangularis aut alia quaeecunque circulari aequalis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The efflux velocity depends on the vertical head (height) and not on the planar shape (circular, square, triangular) of the hole, nor on whether the hole is in the bottom or side of the vessel, provided the effective head is the same and other geometric flow corrections (contraction, oblique approach) are accounted for. Experiments reported confirm these statements and quantify contraction effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective efflux area/vena contraction and practical diameter adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: foramen in fundo vasis, propter obliquos motus partlcularum aquae effluentis, paulo majus esse debet quam prius ... existentiae ejus diametro ad diametrum foraminis ut 5 ad 6, vel 51 ad 6  quam proxime ... experimenta vero constat ... cujus diameter est ad diametrum foraminis illius ut 21 ad 25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents practical corrections for vena contraction: the effective cross-section of the flowing jet just outside the hole is smaller than the hole area; experimental ratios (e.g., 21:25) are given to correct for oblique approach and contraction. This is guidance for applying the ideal efflux theorem to real vessels and estimating the actual discharged volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efflux momentum/force equivalence to weight of a cylinder of base equal to hole and height twice the head
rubrics_metrics.description: vis, qua totus aquae exilientis motus generari potest, aequalis est ponderi cylindricae columnae aquae, cujus basis est foramen EF, & altitudo 2GI vel 2CK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The total momentum (or the effort) required to put the effluent water into motion is equal to the weight of a cylindrical column of water whose base equals the hole area and whose height equals twice the height of the free surface above a reference (as constructed in the proposition). This provides a hydrostatic-mechanical equivalence useful for force/balance calculations and follows from comparing energies/weights in the geometric constructions given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic relations: distribution of weight on vessel bottom vs efflux
rubrics_metrics.description: Pondus aquae totius in vase ABDC est ad ponderis partem, quae in defluxum aquae impenditur, ut summa circulorum AB & EF ad duplum circulum EF. ... pondus aquae totius in vase est ad pondus aquae totam quae fundo perpendiculariter incumbit, ut circulus AB ad differentiam circulorum AB & EF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several corollaries give exact proportional relations between the total weight of water in the vessel, the part of the weight contributing to efflux, and the part supported by the vessel bottom — expressed in terms of areas (circles) of the free surface and the orifice. These are precise hydrostatic bookkeeping relations derived from the geometric constructions and are useful for computing loads on vessel bottoms and the effective driving weight for efflux.
